title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
abstract: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. PODCAST SERIES The Shape of Things to Come Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future. Listen now Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat

title: Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture
abstract: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. title: Better speech synthesis for audiobooks
abstract: Text-to-speech systems — which convert written text into synthetic speech — display impressive naturalness in applications such as chatbots and virtual assistants, where interactions last seconds. But they tend not to fare as well with longer-form content. When applied to audiobooks, for instance, conventional text-to-speech (TTS) models fail to reliably change speaking style between characters, as a human narrator would. This creates two problems for listeners: (1) distinguishing narration from dialogue and (2) identifying which character speaks which lines. To address this problem, the Audible technology team is using controllable TTS, meaning the ability to control dialogue delivery with natural-language speech descriptions (e.g., "speak in an enthusiastic, high-pitched voice"). This allows the TTS model to leverage the deep textual understanding of large language models (LLMs) to synthesize high-quality speech. Our approach involves three key innovations. First, we developed a novel data synthesis pipeline to produce speech data captioned with high-quality descriptions of speech characteristics. Training on this data enables our model to understand captions and produce audio consistent with them at inference time. Second, we created a system that automatically profiles characters in books and identifies their dialogue with 97% accuracy. It also provides captions for that dialogue, which act as stage directions for the model. Third, we used the first two techniques to synthesize audiobooks featuring distinct character voices, improving dialogue differentiation by 3.7 points on a MUSHRA (multiple stimuli with hidden reference and anchor) test, a standardized method where listeners rate audio quality on a scale from 0 to 100. Across tests in both English and Spanish, we observe statistically significant improvement in listening experience for eight out of ten voices. TTS for audiobooks Subtle defects in synthetic speech, such as unnatural prosody or monotone delivery, are tolerable for short stretches but become increasingly grating over time — and audiobook listeners engage with the same voice for 10 to 15 hours per book. This is why off-the-shelf TTS models often fail to produce enjoyable, natural audiobook narrations. Furthermore, general-purpose TTS models are designed to process individual utterances with minimal context. That’s a reasonable approach when responding to questions like "What's the weather today?", but it’s inadequate for audiobooks, where narrative coherence depends on understanding the surrounding story context. A TTS model reading dialogue needs to know whether the speaker is the protagonist confronting an antagonist or a minor character making small talk, information that may only be available in earlier chapters. Finally, general-purpose models struggle to produce character voices in a consistent and natural way across the span of an entire book, often voicing a character in a markedly different way in chapter 1 than in chapter 10. Controllable text-to-speech I. The data synthesis pipeline Whereas conventional TTS models are trained on text-speech pairs, a controllable-TTS model also requires annotations that describe how the speech sounds. The speech in the training set also needs to be highly expressive, covering the wide variety of dimensions — pitch, speaking rate, character voices, emotions, speaking styles, etc. — the model must control. Previous TTS models couldn't handle that kind of expressivity, so most existing training data is neutral in tone. We expanded the training sets through two approaches: new recordings and human captioning of existing audio data. While there are some datasets that include descriptions of prosodic features, each has its own description format: some are long, some are short, and some use single tags. title: The science behind TorchNeuron, Amazon’s new PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium chips
abstract: PyTorch is the one framework that most AI developers use to build their models. It’s a Python library of operations performed on tensors, higher-dimensional analogues of a matrix, or 2-D grid of numbers. Almost all of the crucial features of contemporary AI models, such as input data, model weights, and attention mechanisms, are represented by tensors, and PyTorch drastically simplifies writing code to manipulate them. This week, we announced the availability of TorchNeuron, an open-source backend that translates PyTorch code into operations executable on AWS Trainium systems. PyTorch code that already runs on other accelerators will run on Trainium with minimal or no code changes. TorchNeuron bridges PyTorch and Trainium, and both sides gain from it. PyTorch developers can now run their code on Trainium, which was built from the ground up for large-tensor workloads. They can also tap the AWS Neuron SDK, which includes a profiler that traces each instruction with cycle-level accuracy and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI, pronounced "Nikki"), which enables control almost at the assembly level. TorchNeuron includes several optimizations that enable PyTorch code to run efficiently on Trainium, including caching at multiple levels and an optional “adaptive eager” mode that doesn’t execute individual operations one by one, as is typical in plain eager mode, but instead groups and compiles operations for more efficient execution, approaching fully compiled performance. Much of the innovation behind TorchNeuron, however, is the way its performance was evaluated. AI agents searched through hundreds of thousands of open-source models and categorized them according to their architectural characteristics. This allowed the Annapurna team around Khaled ElGalaind and Sarang Ozarde to identify 841 representative models covering the full spectrum of model architectures. From those models, they also distilled tens of thousands of practically important tensor dimensions, or “shapes”, which were then used to tune and benchmark TorchNeuron’s performance. The result is that PyTorch programmers can trust TorchNeuron to execute their code accurately, efficiently, and most importantly, right out of the box. Runtime optimizations Adaptive eager mode Standard PyTorch has two native execution modes. One is called “eager”, meaning that PyTorch operations are executed immediately, in program order. The other mode is compiled mode, where the programmer selects blocks of code that should be compiled in the traditional sense, meaning that a compiler builds a control-flow graph of the tensor operations and optimizes it. There are many optimization techniques in place today, such as operator fusion to reduce memory traffic and increase locality. Developers often use eager mode when they’re debugging models and compiled mode once they’re confident their code is correct and want it to execute as efficiently as possible. TorchNeuron adds something in-between, an opt-in setting called adaptive eager mode, which offers some of the advantages of compilation but operates on smaller subgraphs. This mode approximates both eager mode’s responsiveness and compiled mode’s performance. At run time, a Python interpreter running on a CPU accumulates instructions it gets from PyTorch ’s operator dispatch and builds small graphs. The graphs are sent to TorchNeuron, which compiles them, caches them, and puts them in a queue for execution. Multiple such graph collections and compilations are happening in parallel, further minimizing the compile time overhead. A key innovation here is that the accumulated graphs, their individual operations, and their input tensor shapes correlate directly with compile time. Larger graphs on larger tensors take longer to compile. Hence, a smart, adaptive algorithm dynamically selects the right subgraphs to maximize the overlap of compile time with the execution of already compiled snippets, effectively hiding all compile time for a great variety

title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
abstract: Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome. Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder . The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result. This post uses Wordle , a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting. In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models . All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository . Solution overview The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect. Figure 1: MTRL on SageMaker AI, where the training job invokes the AgentCore-hosted agent once per rollout to sample the policy model, play the game, and report a reward For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word , and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ) adapter on the policy model. Three design points matter for what follows: The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function. The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring. The reward is outcome-dominant. A solve pays 1.05–1.55 depending on speed, a loss pays -0.5

title: Orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling with AWS CDK
abstract: Updating the Amazon Sagemaker AI real-time endpoint configuration (changing the instance type, instance count, or environment variables) causes deployments through AWS CloudFormation or the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to fail. SageMaker AI requires you to deregister the scalable target before updating the endpoint, but when you deregister it, CloudFormation can’t track the AWS Application Auto Scaling resources. In this post, we show you how to use a reusable CDK construct with AWS CloudFormation custom resources to orchestrate deregister and register auto scaling automatically during endpoint updates. You can update your endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters in a single deployment without manual intervention. Why this problem occurs When you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with native CloudFormation auto scaling resources, then change the endpoint configuration and redeploy, several failure modes emerge. The specific failure depends on what you change and how you work around the issue. Changing the endpoint configuration with auto scaling registered CloudFormation tries to update the endpoint while the scalable target is still registered. SageMaker AI rejects the update with the following error: The variant(s) "[AllTraffic]" must be deregistered as scalable targets with Application Auto Scaling before they can be removed or have their instance type updated. SageMaker AI blocks the endpoint update before CloudFormation reaches the auto scaling resources. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing only the endpoint configuration If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and redeploy with only an endpoint configuration change, the deployment succeeds. However, CloudFormation doesn’t register auto scaling even though it is in the CloudFormation template. Because the auto scaling parameters in the CloudFormation template haven’t changed, CloudFormation doesn’t register the scalable target or re-apply the scaling policy. The endpoint is now running without auto scaling, and there is no error to indicate anything went wrong. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing auto scaling parameters If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS CLI and redeploy with auto scaling parameter changes, CloudFormation tries to update the ScalableTarget resource that no longer exists: Resource of type 'AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget' with identifier 'endpoint/<name>/variant/AllTraffic|sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount|sagemaker' was not found. This failure is notable because the rollback also fails (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED), leaving the stack in a broken state that requires manual intervention in the CloudFormation console to recover. Solution overview You can use this CDK construct to replace the native AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget and AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalingPolicy CloudFormation resources with three custom resources. These custom resources deregister and register auto scaling around the endpoint update with explicit dependency ordering, enforced by node.add_dependency calls in CDK. The full sequence is: Deregister (custom resource): Removes the scalable target before the endpoint update begins. On first deploy, no scalable target exists yet, so the handler handles the error gracefully and continues. Endpoint update (CDK-managed): CDK updates the endpoint resource normally, swapping to the new endpoint configuration. Register Scalable Target (custom resource): Waits for the endpoint to reach InService status, then registers the scalable target. Attach Scaling Policy (custom resource): Waits for the scalable target to be queryable, then applies the target tracking policy. Figure 1: Custom resource orchestration of SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling around a CDK-managed endpoint update. title: Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps
abstract: With Amazon Quick Sight layer maps, you can now plot points and routes, like store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport. Geospatial maps help businesses spot patterns that are tied to location, like how a region is performing or where customers are concentrated. Amazon Quick Sight supports this with multiple map types, including point maps, filled maps, and layer maps. When layer maps first launched , you could upload a GeoJSON file to draw custom shape layers, such as sales territories or districts, and join those shapes to a dataset. That handled regions and boundaries well, but it didn’t cover the individual locations inside them or the routes running between them. Layer maps now support two more geometry types from the same GeoJSON workflow: Point and LineString . Points mark specific locations, such as individual store or facility sites. A LineString traces the route between locations, like a delivery path or a flight between airports. Amazon Quick Sight , the business intelligence (BI) capability of Amazon Quick , is a unified BI service. It delivers modern interactive dashboards, natural language querying, pixel-perfect reports, machine learning (ML) insights, and embedded analytics at scale. Amazon Quick brings together AI agents for business insights, research, and automation in one integrated experience, helping you work smarter and faster while maintaining security and access policies. In this post, we walk through the dataset and GeoJSON structure that layer maps require. We also explain how points and lines work in a layer map visual and when to choose each. Finally, we cover advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering geometries, and updating GeoJSON files programmatically. Dataset structure considerations A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a Quick Sight dataset, and a shared key joins the two. How you structure each one determines what the map can show. This section covers what you need before you start and how a GeoJSON file is organized. Prerequisites The following are the prerequisites that you need before creating a layer map in Quick Sight: A GeoJSON file describing your geometry. A Quick Sight dataset holding the metrics and dimensions. A join key shared between the Quick Sight dataset and the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON file must be saved in .geojson format, with a maximum supported file size of 100 MB. Structure of the GeoJSON file GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for describing geographic features such as points and lines. { "type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [{ "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [88.4, 22.6] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }, { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "LineString", "coordinates": [ [88.2, 22.4], [88.9, 23.1], [89.5, 22.8], [90.1, 23.6] ] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }] } The structure of the file is as follows: FeatureCollection is the whole file. It has a type of FeatureCollection and a features array. Feature is a single map element. It carries a geometry (the shape) and a properties object, which holds the join key. geometry has a type (Point, LineString, or Polygon) and its coordinates . The coordinates hold a single [longitude, latitude] position for a Point , and an ordered list of positions for a LineString . Configuring the Quick Sight dataset and its GeoJSON In Quick Sight, when you configure a layer in a layer map visual, there are two primary settings to consider. The first is the Geometry type to visualize , which sets which geometry from the GeoJSON file renders: Points, Lines, or Polygons. A layer renders one geometry type at a time, so when a file mixes types like the preceding example, only Features of the selected type appear on the map. The second is matching the Shape file key field to the Dataset key field , which links each Feature in the GeoJSON to a row in your Quick Sight dataset. title: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations
abstract: Plant breeding decisions depend on data that spans genomics, field trials, imagery, environmental conditions, and model outputs. Bayer Crop Science runs hundreds of machine learning (ML) model configurations against this data across crops, regions, and teams, and each run needs to be repeatable and governed. To meet that requirement, Bayer built the Connected Decision Engine (CDE), a system for deploying, orchestrating, monitoring, and reusing ML workflows. CDE gives breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and data engineers a consistent way to run analytics while preserving execution history and operational controls. As adoption grew, the bottleneck moved from running workflows to understanding them. Explaining a result meant piecing together context from APIs, documentation, metadata stores, dashboards, and logs. A user who wanted to know why a workflow failed, what a model did, or where a result came from still had to know which system to inspect. To close that gap, Bayer built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent, natural language interface over CDE. A supervisor agent routes each question to a specialist agent, the specialist retrieves context from the relevant system, and the user receives an answer without navigating the operational stack. In its first phase, ADE resolves about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop. ADE runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , an AWS service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore let the team focus on agent behavior instead of building and operating its own agent hosting, session isolation, and tool access layer. Three AgentCore capabilities drove that choice: a managed runtime that isolates each user session, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped tool access through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, that keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code, and a framework-agnostic design that let the team bring its own LangGraph orchestration and choice of models. To prepare for launch and to operate ADE afterward, Bayer engaged AWS Unified Operations . The engagement provided a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and a generative AI Domain Specialist Engineer (DSE), who worked as an extension of the ADE team from design through production. The TAM, as Bayer’s strategic advisor, brought an established understanding of Bayer’s operating model and business priorities. The DSE brought generative AI domain expertise on AWS. In three technical standups each week, the team reviewed and made design decisions. The DSE built working knowledge of the ADE workload and how the Bayer team operates, so technical guidance reflected both AWS service behavior and Bayer’s context. This post follows that journey: the ADE architecture, five design decisions made during the build, the work to prepare the platform for production, and how it is operated after launch. Architecture overview ADE is organized into four layers: the user experience, agent orchestration, specialist agents, and the tools and data sources those agents call (Figure 1). Users reach ADE through a React web front end, and requests pass through an identity proxy for Microsoft Entra ID before they reach the agents. GitHub Actions builds the agent container images, pushes them to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) , and deploys them to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the agents, and because the runtime is framework-agnostic, the team runs its own LangGraph-based orchestration on it directly. The team chose LangGraph for its explicit graph-based control flow and checkpointing for multi-step workflows. LangGraph orchestrates the workflow, with a Supervisor Agent as the entry point that classifies each request, selects a specialist, and combines results when a question spans domains. The data plane is separated by responsibility.

title: Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine
abstract: Amazon Polly Generative engine now offers more natural and accurate speech output. We’re introducing an upgrade to the Amazon Polly Generative engine that delivers more expressive, more accurate speech output with low latency. The upgrade adds 14 new voices across 9 locales, including general availability of Generative voices in Hindi and Finnish for the first time. The upgrade is now generally available in production. Importantly, this is a drop-in upgrade for existing generative voices. Voice names and API calls are unchanged, so your existing applications continue to work as they do today. Amazon Polly is a fully managed AWS service that converts text into natural-sounding speech for contact centers, large language model (LLM)-based agentic applications, media and entertainment, e-learning, accessibility, and other applications that require reliable voice output at scale. Hear the difference You can use sample audio to evaluate the improvements directly. The more natural, authentic, and expressive voices. Hear how Tiffany welcomes you in a delightful tone. “Hi there! I’m Tiffany, one of Polly’s generative voices. I was built to sound natural, expressive, and a little bit delightful. What should we talk about?” Accurate speech generation for numbers, currency, addresses, and so on. Kenneth reads back an order confirmation, including the tracking number, date and time, currency and address accurately. “Thanks for calling. Your order, number 4471 9902 ships today to 85 Harbor View Drive, Apartment 4B, Portland, Oregon 97209. It should arrive on Thursday, October 22nd, between 9 AM and 1 PM. Your total was $1,284.50 and your confirmation code is K-7-Q-2-X-9.” Net new languages. Arjun and Kiara for Hindi, and Suvi for Finnish. Hindi and Finnish are generally available for the first time on the Amazon Polly Generative engine. Arjun : नमस्कार, आप सुन रहे हैं आज की मुख्य ख़बरें। देश के कई हिस्सों में मानसून की विदाई के साथ मौसम सुहाना हो गया है। (Hello, you’re listening to today’s top stories. As the monsoon retreats across much of the country, the weather has turned pleasant.) Kiara : नमस्ते! मेरा नाम कियारा है। आइए, आज मैं आपको एक छोटी सी कहानी सुनाती हूँ।(Hello! My name is Kiara. Come, let me tell you a little story today.) Suvi : Majakanvartija ei ollut nähnyt laivaa yhteentoista päivään. Sitten, vähän puolenyön jälkeen, horisontissa välähti yksi ainoa valo. Kerran. Kahdesti. Ja sitten, uskomatonta kyllä, se vilkutti takaisin hänen nimensä. (The lighthouse keeper hadn’t seen a ship in eleven days. Then, just after midnight, a single light blinked on the horizon. Once. Twice. And then, impossibly, it blinked back his name.) Different styles of speech delivery based on textual context. Powered by the new Amazon Polly Generative engine, the voices can reflect emotion and prosody even better based on the text input, without manual setup. Neutral : “Your package arrived early.” Uncertainty : “So, um… your package arrived early. I think?” Surprised : “Wait, what? Your package arrived early?” New voices, languages, and Region availability A larger catalog overall for Amazon Polly Generative engine – Totaling 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales. 14 new voices across 9 locales – US English (Kenneth, Nate), Australian English (Russell, Curtis), Indian English (Kiara, Arjun), German (Tina), US Spanish (Carlos), Brazilian Portuguese (Leo, Carolina), Korean (Hyunduk), Hindi (Kiara, Arjun) and Finnish (Suvi). Built for production-ready speech workflows for enterprise The upgraded Amazon Polly Generative engine uses a standard Amazon Polly API call to build your speech applications. title: How IskayPet unified corporate knowledge with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases
abstract: IskayPet’s office teams had a knowledge challenge. Answers to everyday operational questions, such as a return policy, a veterinary protocol, or an onboarding step, lived in hundreds of Microsoft SharePoint documents spread across four languages and three countries. Finding the right information in large document repositories took a long time. Every new store, country, or procedure made the problem bigger. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is the usual way to solve this. But running RAG in production normally means operating vector databases, embedding pipelines, and ingestion jobs yourself. In this post, we show how IskayPet, a leading pet care company in Iberia, built a corporate knowledge assistant on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases. The assistant answers employee questions across retail operations, veterinary care, people and onboarding, and procurement, in four languages and across three countries, with no RAG infrastructure to manage. The team built the whole solution, from the store-facing frontend to the AWS architecture and deployment, using Kiro with Claude Haiku 4.5. We cover the architecture, the SharePoint integration, the retrieval configuration decisions, and the results in production. About IskayPet IskayPet is a leading pet care company in Iberia. It operates more than 330 stores across Spain, Portugal, and France under the Kiwoko, Tiendanimal, Kivet, Clinicanimal and Animalis brands. With more than 4,500 employees and 7 million customers, IskayPet runs operations that span retail, veterinary clinics, animal care, procurement, and people and onboarding. Each area has its own policies and procedures, in Spanish, Portuguese, French, and English. The challenge Across every business area, IskayPet office staff searched hundreds of SharePoint documents by hand to answer operational questions about procedures, policies, contracts, and onboarding. With operations in three countries and four languages, this took real time, and the answer was often outdated or wrong. There was no reliable way to query corporate knowledge, and the problem grew with every country, area, or document added. IskayPet needed a solution that could do the following: Answer natural-language questions grounded in their own corporate documents. Work across four languages without maintaining separate systems. Route each question to the right body of knowledge (an area, a country) without cross-contamination. Scale to new areas and countries without re-architecting. Cite its sources so employees can trust and verify answers. Reuse their existing SharePoint repositories without a costly migration. Why Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases IskayPet chose Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases for its managed RAG infrastructure, which removed the need to run vector stores, embeddings, or ingestion pipelines. The main reasons were: Managed RAG: Amazon Bedrock handles data ingestion, multimodal parsing, vector storage, embedding generation, and retrieval. IskayPet pays only for what it stores and retrieves. Native SharePoint connector: The connector ingests documents directly from IskayPet’s existing SharePoint environment, which avoided a data migration. With advanced indexing enabled, it also processes content from images embedded in documents. Built-in hybrid search: Combining semantic and keyword (BM25) search at no extra cost recovers exact terms, such as product codes and references, that pure semantic search can miss. Managed reranking: Retrieved passages are reordered by relevance at no additional charge. Document-level access control: The knowledge base can enforce the source system’s own permissions at retrieval time, so a query returns only passages from documents the requesting user is already allowed to read. This lets IskayPet reuse SharePoint permissions instead of rebuilding an authorization model. Model flexibility: IskayPet can start with a cost-effective model and change it later without rewriting infrastructure. Native RAG

title: Announcing new ways to customize models with SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs
abstract: Companies getting real results from AI aren’t only using foundation models (FMs) off the shelf. They’re customizing open-weight models using post-training techniques such as reinforcement learning. A model trained on your business context, product catalog, or clinical vocabulary will be more accurate for your task and cost less to run. When you build agents, your data, workflows, evaluations, and success criteria also shape how the model behaves. However, model customization is difficult. You must choose the right technique, set up and manage GPU infrastructure, and, for agents, build environments for multi-turn reinforcement learning. We launched Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to solve these challenges, and today, we’re expanding it with the general availability launch of training sessions. With training sessions you get control over the post-training logic without managing the underlying infrastructure. You write and coordinate the training loop, including custom loss functions or reward signals. SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. Customize without the hassles of infrastructure management With SageMaker AI serverless model customization, you don’t choose instance types, manage clusters, or write distributed training configuration. We didn’t want to limit you . You can use techniques such as SFT, DPO, RLVR, RLAIF, or multi-turn RL. You can choose how much of the model to update with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) or full fine-tuning and chain techniques together through continuous customization. We didn’t want you to waste time . Our SageMaker AI training sessions cookbook provides examples and use cases, along with model customization agent skills. You describe your use case, and the agent handles data prep, technique choice, training, evaluation, and deployment. The agent works where you work, in SageMaker Studio, Kiro, Claude Code, Codex, or GitHub Copilot. “We adopted SageMaker AI Serverless Training Sessions to build a healthcare claim-denial triage model, and the experience validated the platform from day one. The low-level API surface, direct control over the forward and backward passes, sampling, and the optimizer step gave our scientists the fine-grained control they need to pursue reinforcement learning on a demanding, accuracy-critical use case. Training Sessions gives us the right primitives to push toward production-grade performance.” — Rob Gontarek, Senior Vice President, Data Science, ImagineSoftware Write your own post-training loop One important shift in agent training is toward multi-turn reinforcement learning. For example, an agent that books travel, triages support tickets, or runs a multi-step research task needs several rounds of interaction before you can judge whether it reached the right outcome. However, the training loop can get complicated quickly. You may train the model on one set of infrastructure, run inference on another to generate responses, score those responses, and feed the results into the next update. Each stage needs different compute, and connecting them across separate tools and clusters adds work. SageMaker AI already offers multi-turn RL as a managed, serverless technique. But we heard from customers who wanted to define their own loss functions, shape reward signals, or RL stages in one loop. Training sessions give you that flexibility. “With SageMaker AI Serverless Training Sessions, we fine-tuned gpt-oss-20b for agentic, multi-turn tool calling against our Amazon Neptune knowledge graph — and the platform handled the infrastructure for us. Setup just worked, with no manual tuning and no out-of-memory wrangling. Checkpoint-and-resume was a standout: resuming from an exact step was completely reliable. It gave our developers the flexibility they wanted while taking the operational burden off their plate.” — Nitin Wagh, CEO, Karini AI How it works Your code runs the training loop and reward function

title: Write your own training loop — without managing GPUs — with Amazon SageMaker training session APIs
abstract: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) today usually forces a tradeoff between training loop control and operational simplicity. With fully managed services you select a base model, provide data and hyperparameters, and the service owns everything else, which works well when a standard, prepackaged recipe fits your problem. Less managed services give you more control, but you also manage more of the underlying infrastructure and training frameworks. Sometimes a standard recipe isn’t enough: you need a custom loss or data curriculum for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), your own preference optimization, a reinforcement learning (RL) reward function, or an alignment algorithm published last week. As soon as you need to shape the training procedure yourself, you take on that infrastructure work to gain algorithmic freedom. Today, serverless model customization in Amazon SageMaker AI expands with training session APIs, which remove that tradeoff by drawing the abstraction boundary one level lower. Instead of abstracting away the algorithm, they abstract away the compute. Operations like forward_backward() , optim_step() , and sample() become SageMaker API calls that you compose into whatever procedure your technique requires: SFT, preference optimization, RL, or something new. The calls target a live, stateful session, so the model stays loaded on the GPUs across steps, and you drive as many calls as you need against it. The service handles runtime setup, distributed execution, gradient synchronization, fault recovery, tenant isolation, and the operations of running GPUs at scale. You write the training loop, and SageMaker AI runs the infrastructure. Alongside the service, we’re releasing the SageMaker training sessions cookbook , a set of ready-to-run SFT and RL recipes that you can use as blueprints for your own training loops. In this post, we introduce the programming model and the three SDK clients, and show where training session APIs fit among the model training and customization options in SageMaker AI. We then take apart a minimal RL loop on grade-school math problems (GSM8K) to show how the operations fit together and finish with a real-world workload from the cookbook: reinforcement learning on competitive programming problems, where generated code is graded by running it against unit tests. What are SageMaker AI training session APIs? With SageMaker AI training session APIs, you can drive a live, GPU-backed session from your own Python process on your local machine. You call the operations, and SageMaker AI runs them on managed accelerators loaded with your chosen base model plus your Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter. There’s no config file describing the whole job up front and no cluster creation step. You control what happens at each step, interactively, from code, so you can iterate and debug quickly. The division of responsibilities looks like this: You focus on You write SageMaker AI handles Your data, RL environments, agents, and algorithm A Python training loop that calls operations such as forward_backward() , optim_step() , and sample() for the steps that need GPUs GPU allocation, model and LoRA loading, distributed execution, fault recovery, checkpoint storage, security The API is organized around three clients in the SageMaker Python SDK , created in sequence. A ServiceClient holds the platform-level settings (execution role, model package group, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) output location, and optionally an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key and virtual private cloud (VPC) configuration, which you can also override per session) and starts a session. The ServiceClient instantiates a TrainingClient (training and checkpointing operations such as forward , forward_backward , optim_step , and save_weights_for_sampler ), which in turn instantiates a SamplingClient ( sample and compute_logprobs , for generation and scoring during rollouts and evaluation). title: Deploy AI in a HIPAA-eligible environment with Amazon Quick
abstract: Healthcare organizations want the same thing from AI that every other business wants: faster answers, less manual work, and insights that reach decision-makers in time to act on them. However, what makes the healthcare industry different is that the data is uniquely complex, deeply contextual, and strictly regulated. So this post starts with a few definitions to set the foundation for everything that follows. Protected Health Information (PHI) is any information that identifies a person and relates to their health, care, or payment for care, such as a medical note, a claim, or a member ID. When software touches PHI, it falls under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), the federal law that governs how PHI data is accessed, secured, and audited. Agentic AI changes what it means for software to “touch PHI.” A traditional analytics tool reads data and returns a response. An agentic workspace like Amazon Quick might go further. For example, its chat agents work across both unstructured content, such as clinical notes and appeals letters, and structured data, such as claims and member records. Agents might retrieve data from both unstructured and structured sources, call other systems through connectors, and complete multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf. Connectors are pre-built integrations that let Amazon Quick securely read from and take action in your external systems, such as Slack , Microsoft Outlook , Salesforce , Atlassian Jira , and Microsoft SharePoint . You can also add your own custom tools through Model Context Protocol (MCP). Only connectors authorized within your organization are visible. When a chat agent can both read and act on PHI, you need sufficient governance: deterministic guardrails, a behavioral audit trail of what the agent did, and clear accountability for actions taken without a person in the loop. To support that governance, Amazon Quick exposes ACL-aware retrieval, chat and feedback logging, and controls over what each chat agent is allowed to do. Amazon Quick is a HIPAA -eligible service. This eligibility applies across the Amazon Quick web, desktop, and mobile clients, subject to the shared responsibility model and your configuration. This post, however, focuses on the capabilities of the Amazon Quick web version, which you access through your browser. In this post, we start with the foundations: who HIPAA applies to and the difference between HIPAA-eligible and HIPAA-compliant. We then introduce Amazon Quick as a platform and the two data flows for PHI (unstructured and structured). From there, we cover what Amazon Quick provides for regulated environments and what it doesn’t, walk through a fictional health plan (AnyCompany) deployment, and distill the best practices and irreversible decisions you should make up front. We close with a step-by-step implementation guide, a conclusion, and resources for deeper reading. Who does HIPAA apply to? HIPAA reaches further than hospitals and clinics. Under the law, two categories of organizations carry obligations, and most AI projects touch both. Covered entities (CEs) Health plans – Health insurance companies, HMOs, employer-sponsored plans, Medicare, and Medicaid. Healthcare clearinghouses – Organizations that process nonstandard health information into standard electronic formats. Healthcare providers – Doctors, clinics, hospitals, pharmacies, nursing homes, and any provider that transmits health information electronically. Business associates (BAs) A business associate is any person or entity, outside the covered entity’s workforce, that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits protected health information (PHI) on the covered entity’s behalf. Common examples include cloud service providers, IT vendors, billing companies, data analytics firms, claims processors, law firms, and consulting firms. Subcontractors who handle PHI on behalf of another business associate are themselves business associates. Covered entities and business

title: Stream low-latency speech from AI agents using Kokoro TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: A customer asks an AI voice agent a question and waits. The agent already has an answer, it’s midway through generating a long, multi-paragraph response, but the customer hears nothing for five seconds. By the time an answer arrives, the customer is frustrated, confused, and no longer paying attention. Text-to-speech integrations create exactly that gap. A one-sentence response might generate in 600 milliseconds, but the full response takes five seconds, and the integration waits for all of it before synthesis starts. This post shows how to close that gap. We stream each sentence to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech (TTS) model on Amazon SageMaker AI as soon as an agent produces it, so synthesis begins on sentence one instead of the finished response. Getting that audio back to a browser needs its own solution too, so we also cover both transports for doing it and what each costs in practice. Solution overview This solution closes the gap by streaming synthesis alongside generation instead of waiting for it to finish. As the agent produces each sentence, that sentence streams immediately to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech model, so audio playback can start before the agent finishes speaking its full response. Kokoro-82M holds only 82 million parameters, small enough to run cheaply on a single mid-tier GPU instance. That keeps both latency and inference cost low for a voice agent handling real traffic. Kokoro-82M runs in a custom container on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, on an ml.g5.xlarge GPU instance. The container exposes two routes: POST /invocations , which streams a response for one complete input, and WS /invocations-bidirectional-stream , which keeps one connection open across many messages in both directions. The following diagram shows the request path from client to model: Figure 1: Request path from the client to the SageMaker AI real-time endpoint over a bidirectional stream Prerequisites Before you begin, you need: An AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI endpoints; AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore; AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles; and an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository, including at minimum the sagemaker:CreateEndpoint , sagemaker:CreateEndpointConfig , sagemaker:CreateModel , sagemaker:InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream , and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream actions. The sample container pins an older PyTorch with a known advisory ( PYSEC-2026-2286 , fixed in torch 2.10.0). Review and upgrade the pin before any non-proof-of-value use. AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) v2 , installed and bootstrapped in your target account and AWS Region. A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint deployed from a container that declares the com.amazonaws.sagemaker.capabilities.bidirectional-streaming=true Docker label. Python 3.12 or later, uv , and Docker to build the container image (the underlying HTTP/2 client only ships pre-built wheels for Python 3.12 and newer). The AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) with support for invoke_endpoint_with_bidirectional_stream . Familiarity with WebSockets and Starlette or a comparable ASGI framework. The deployment code from the GitHub repository referenced in this post. Walkthrough The walkthrough first deploys the endpoint and agent, then works through the client-side changes that make incremental streaming work end to end. Deploy the endpoint and agent The Kokoro-82M endpoint and the agent runtime deploy through two CLI tools, each wrapping its own AWS CDK stacks: uv run speech-infra deploy kokoro-82m uv run agent-infra deploy --bedrock-model-id <your-bedrock-model-id> speech-infra deploy provisions the Kokoro-82M endpoint. This includes the foundation and model-cache stacks that create the underlying IAM roles and sync the model’s weights into Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). title: Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: A traffic spike hits your self-hosted text-to-speech (TTS) endpoint, and requests start queueing. Latency climbs past your service level objective (SLO) right when the most callers are listening. The auto scaling policy behind that endpoint was supposed to prevent this, but the target value it scales on was a guess, and guesses like that fail silently until real traffic proves them wrong. Get that number wrong, and it’s paid for in one of two ways, and neither shows up as an alarm. Guess too conservative, and the fleet runs GPU instances that sit mostly idle. That cost lands on every invoice but never trips an incident report. Guess too aggressive, and the fleet carries a risk nobody sees. Each instance holds more concurrent requests than it can serve inside its latency promise. Nothing looks wrong until a real traffic spike pushes queueing time past the SLO. That happens right when the most callers are listening. That’s the hidden gap. A policy that looks fine on the console can already be failing the people it’s supposed to serve. In this post, we deploy Kokoro-82M , an 82-million-parameter TTS model, as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stacks handle the deployment. We replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint. Q_max is the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and T_total is how long a scale-out takes end to end. We derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Every number in this post comes from an actual deployment and measurement run of the aws-samples repository referenced in this post. Why default auto scaling metrics don’t work for TTS Most public guidance on Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling targets short synchronous request/response calls, or large language model (LLM) serving, where the natural metric is tokens generated per second. TTS synthesis fits neither pattern: a single request holds a connection open for several seconds with no token-generation loop to attach a metric to. Kokoro-82M is non-autoregressive, a StyleTTS2 derivative with an ISTFTNet decoder, trained adversarially rather than by autoregressive next-token prediction or iterative denoising. It produces a full utterance from one duration-aligned pass. There’s no generation loop to instrument with a per-token metric in the first place. What determines whether a TTS instance is overloaded is simpler than it sounds: how many requests are queued and executing on it right now. The deployed policy scales on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel , a native metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes itself rather than one this project’s own container code has to emit. Scaling on a metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes removes an entire class of failure where a custom metric configuration looks correct on paper but nothing is actually publishing to it. ConcurrentRequestsPerModel publishes a Maximum statistic over a 10-second window, a different quantity from the mean in-flight count a benchmarking client measures directly. The tooling accounts for this. At every rung of the concurrency ladder it measures both quantities against the same load and records the ratio between them. It then uses that ratio to convert the client-measured threshold into Amazon CloudWatch units before writing it into the deployable configuration. For the Kokoro-82M run in this post, the measured ratio came out to exactly 1.0 at every rung, so the client-measured and Amazon CloudWatch-reported thresholds match directly. title: How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC
abstract: Every engineering team knows the ritual, and Rescale was no exception. A nightly test suite fails. An on-call engineer pulls the logs, classifies the root cause, and routes it to the right team, only to repeat the process the next morning. At scale, across distributed services and dozens of repositories, this ritual becomes a full-time job hiding inside an on-call rotation. Rescale is the digital engineering platform built for the AI era. R&D and engineering teams across aerospace, automotive, energy, life sciences, semiconductor, and manufacturing use the Rescale platform to accelerate innovation, bringing intelligent HPC, advanced modeling and simulation, agentic digital engineering, and AI physics together on a single platform. Beyond coding, Rescale uses AI across the engineering lifecycle, from planning and design through implementation, testing, review, and operations, while keeping engineers accountable for the result. AI can propose and execute, but people define scope, validate the work, and approve production changes. Engineers can then focus on architecture, product judgment, and the context required to operate complex distributed systems. In this post, we show how Rescale used the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework on AWS to build an intelligent triage agent. They went from problem definition to staging deployment in five days, and to production within weeks. The post also covers how Rescale is extending AI-DLC across their engineering organization. The challenge As Rescale’s platform grew, so did the operational overhead of keeping it running. Engineers were spending significant time on a repetitive but critical task: classifying automated end-to-end test failures. Hundreds of test cases run in the suite, and when failures appeared, every alert, bug report, and escalation needed to be classified, prioritized, and routed to the right team. After routing, engineers would need to gather evidence from multiple logging and monitoring systems, along with several source repositories before debugging could even begin. Passing end-to-end tests were required to deploy services to production and thus debugging these system failures was in the critical path to getting new changes to production. In the manual workflow, engineers moved from the test report to logs, historical patterns, and source code to classify failures and identify the likely owning team. Because these integration tests gate weekly production releases, unresolved failures could pull several teams into hours of coordination before a deployment was allowed to proceed. The team had a clear idea of what a solution looked like: an intelligent agent that could classify and route issues automatically. What they were looking for was a structured way to go from that understanding to a working system in production, with enough structure to extend the approach to other use cases afterward. Why Rescale chose AI-DLC Rescale’s triage agent was a well-scoped problem with a tight timeline. The team needed a development approach that could move at that pace without skipping the architectural decisions that would determine whether the system worked in production. The AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) is an open source, AI-centric methodology for software development built around two ideas: AI executes, humans decide: AI generates work plans, writes code, and proposes architecture, but it surfaces decision points and asks clarifying questions rather than guessing. Humans validate and steer at each step. Team sessions replace async handoffs: Instead of one person building alone and requesting review later, AI-DLC uses focused group sessions: Mob Elaboration (defining requirements together) and Mob Construction (building together while AI handles implementation). Decisions happen in real time. AI-DLC fit because the hard part wasn’t writing code. It was making sure the AI understood what the team wanted to build. In mob sessions, Rescale engineers answered

title: Securing Quick access from corporate networks with AWS PrivateLink
abstract: When enterprise data sits behind a corporate firewall or in a private on-premises data center, there’s no direct network path from AWS, even though the AI agents and dashboards in Amazon Quick can query virtually any data source. Administrators must make sure their sensitive enterprise data isn’t exposed to the public internet while being accessible for AI-driven insights and actions. For many enterprises, routing traffic over the public internet introduces unacceptable risk. Regulatory frameworks such as HIPAA, FedRAMP, and PCI-DSS often mandate that sensitive data remain within controlled network boundaries. Even where compliance isn’t the primary driver, exposing internal data paths increases the attack surface, complicates audit trails and introduces variable latency that can degrade the user experience. This walkthrough shows you how to connect on-premises data sources to Amazon Quick privately, without traffic traversing the public internet. It assumes you already have AWS Direct Connect or an AWS Site-to-Site VPN linking your on-premises environment to your virtual private cloud (VPC). From that foundation, we configure VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink so that Quick can reach your private resources over the AWS backbone, then layer security groups and VPC endpoint policies for defense in depth. By the end, you will have a network architecture that keeps traffic between Quick and your on-premises data sources off the public internet, reducing the attack surface, providing consistent low-latency connectivity, and giving you a clear audit trail for compliance. Amazon Quick and establishing private network connectivity Amazon Quick is an AI-powered workspace that brings search, analytics, research, and automation into a single conversational experience. Understanding which components reach your private network, and how, determines the architecture in the sections that follow. Data access in Amazon Quick falls into two paths. User-facing traffic covers anyone opening the Quick console, interacting with a dashboard, making an API call, or using Quick Desktop. All this routes through VPC endpoints (see VPC endpoints for user and API access), keeping user sessions off the public internet. Data-fetching traffic is when Quick itself reaches into your network to pull data. This is handled by VPC connections (see VPC connections for data source access), and it’s where most of the architectural decisions lie. The features and integrations that initiate data-fetching connections are: Amazon Quick Sight queries on-premises databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and others) directly through ENIs placed in your VPC. This is the heaviest consumer of VPC connections. Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate are separate automation features. Flows handle repeatable tasks. Automate handles complex, multi-system orchestration with human-in-the-loop. Both invoke action connectors, including MCP servers hosted privately in your VPC. Any workflow that calls an internal API routes through this path. Quick Agents underpin all conversational interactions and can invoke action connectors directly. When a custom agent calls a privately hosted MCP server or internal API, traffic flows through the VPC connection. Amazon Quick Index builds a unified search layer across connected sources such as Confluence, SharePoint, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). For data inside your VPC or on premises, knowledge base VPC connections are currently supported only for Amazon Redshift. Sources such as Confluence, SharePoint, Box, Google Drive, OneDrive, and Amazon S3 can’t use a Quick VPC connection today (see Supported VPC data sources ). You can still restrict Amazon S3 bucket access to a VPC endpoint through a bucket policy, which is a separate mechanism. title: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them
abstract: Building a multi-agent system is now pretty straightforward. Taking it to production is where the real challenges begin. Thanks to open source frameworks and cloud services, you can set up an agent in a matter of days. A few tool calls, a few lines of prompt, and you have something that looks impressive. But the moment teams try to move beyond a pilot and into real business applications, they hit a familiar wall. If you’ve ever tried to put an agent into production, these frustrations will sound familiar: Why doesn’t the agent follow our business logic, skip validation steps, or catch edge cases? You tweak the prompt, add more examples, swap out the model. The same problems keep coming back. That’s because agents don’t follow a fixed sequence of instructions. They make their own judgments based on context. Instructions alone aren’t enough. You need to design how the agent thinks, when it verifies, and what it does when things go wrong. This is exactly why it’s become critical to go beyond prompt engineering alone and design the agent’s entire cognitive architecture and execution flow. To tackle these challenges head-on, the AWS Solutions Architecture team built Deep Insight , a production-grade multi-agent system. In this post series, we share what the team learned firsthand while building Deep Insight across three posts. We will walk through how we applied Context Engineering techniques proposed by Anthropic (multi-agent architecture, structured note-taking, human-in-the-loop, and more) in a real production environment. We also cover the trade-offs we encountered along the way (with code) and the operational insights we gained from deploying and running this agent on AWS. Blog series overview Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them. Part 2: Beyond the context window: Context Engineering techniques and how Deep Insight applied them. Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. This is Part 1 of a three-part series. It defines the five core challenges any production multi-agent system must solve and shows how each layer of the stack addresses them, from Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Application Load Balancer , and AWS Fargate . Parts 2 and 3 cover Context Engineering and production deployment. Introducing Deep Insight Deep Insight is a multi-agent system that turns complex data analysis into automated insights. Given a CSV file and a natural-language prompt, a hierarchy of specialized agents (Coordinator, Planner, Supervisor, Coder, Validator, Reporter, and Tracker) collaborates on the analysis. Together they load the data, run analyses, generate charts, validate calculations, and produce a professional report (.docx) with citations. We will explore the architecture in detail later. First, let’s see it in action. For the demo, we feed advertising data from a fictional food company, Yummy Food ( yummy-food-market.csv ) with a column definitions file ( column_definitions.json ), and provide the prompt: Analyze this from a sales and marketing perspective, generate charts and insights, and produce a .docx report. Deep Insight generates an analysis plan, presents it to the user for approval, and, once approved, executes the analysis.
